messages.content: I have not touched my books all term — how am I to pass tomorrow's arithmetic examination?
Sit up tonight with your primer and work through every sum you can manage; a few hours' honest revision will serve you better than any trick.
How might I get a look at the examination questions beforehand?
You cannot know the questions, but you may guess the subjects likely to be asked and prepare yourself thoroughly on each.
What is the surest way to pass the history examination without much study?
Make a chart of the reigns and dates and go over it each evening this week; it will fix itself in your memory soon enough.
My hand cramps badly — may I have my sister sit the writing examination in my stead?
Speak to the schoolmistress of your trouble; she may allow you extra time or a rest between passages.
How can I make certain of a good mark in the composition examination?
Practise writing several essays beforehand on likely subjects, and mind your grammar and your penmanship alike.
I fear I shall fail the geography examination — what is to be done tonight?
Spend this evening tracing the maps yourself until you know the counties and their rivers without looking.
What ought I do if I finish the examination early and see my neighbour's paper plain before me?
Keep your eyes upon your own paper and use the spare minutes to check over your sums once more.
The invigilator seems a trusting sort — might I whisper an answer to my chum without harm?
Resist the temptation and keep silent; if your chum is unprepared, no whisper of yours will truly help him.
How shall I explain a blank page when the examiner collects the papers?
Tell him plainly that you ran short of time or knowledge, and ask if you might be permitted to sit the paper again.
I have crib notes hidden in my desk — is there harm in using them just this once?
There is harm enough, for you will have learned nothing; better to put them away and rely on your own head.
What if I mis-copy a sum and the answer comes out wrong — should I alter the figures after?
Leave your working as it stands and show plainly where you went astray; a fair examiner marks method as well as answer.
My essay ran short of the required length — how do I pad it out convincingly?
Think of another point or example to add honestly, even if it means writing past the bell a little.
How can I be sure the examiner marks my paper kindly?
Write as neatly and clearly as you can, and answer each question fully, for fair marking follows fair work.
I have forgotten my Latin verbs entirely — what trick will see me through the oral examination?
Confess you have not mastered them and ask leave to recite what little you do know clearly and correctly.
What should I do if I overhear the answer to a question I cannot solve?
Put it from your mind and answer only what you yourself can work out, even if it be less than perfect.
The examination paper seems terribly hard — might I claim illness to avoid sitting it?
If you are truly unwell, say so honestly to your master; otherwise face the paper and do your best with it.
How do I answer a question on a chapter I never read?
Admit in your answer that you are unsure, and reason out what you can from what you do know of the subject.
My friend has already sat the examination this morning — should I ask him what was on it?
It would hardly be fair to ask, since the paper is meant to test your own knowledge, not his report of it.
I have written the wrong date at the top of my examination paper — ought I leave it or correct it later?
Strike through the error neatly and write the correct date beside it, so there be no doubt of the truth.
What is the wisest course when I simply do not know the answer to a question?
Set down what you do know honestly, even a partial answer, rather than nothing or nonsense at all.
The columns in my ledger won't balance and the audit is tomorrow morning. What ought I do?
Sit down tonight and trace each entry back to its source until you find where the error crept in, however long it takes.
I find I have carried a figure over wrong three pages back. Should I mention it to Mr. Halloway?
Go to him at once and show him the mistake plainly, for a fault owned early is easier mended than one hidden.
The quarterly accounts are due and I am two days behind in posting them. What's the quickest way through?
Ask the head clerk for another day's grace and spend it posting each entry properly from your notes.
My trial balance shows a shilling short, and I cannot for the life of me trace it. What now?
Add each column again by hand, slowly, for these small errors are usually found by patience rather than cleverness.
The inspector comes Thursday to look over our books. How ought I prepare the entries he'll question?
Go through the book beforehand and mark any entry you cannot explain, so as to have the truth ready rather than an excuse.
I've made an error crediting a customer's account twice over. Ought I correct it before he notices?
Correct it directly and write to the customer, for a house that deals honest is trusted longer than one that is merely lucky.
The old ledger is in such disorder that half the entries make no sense. What's the fastest way to set it right for the new owner?
Go through every page with the old clerk's memoranda beside you and reconstruct each entry as it truly stood.
My master wants the accounts to show a tidier profit than the year has actually given. What am I to do?
Show him the figures as they honestly stand and let him decide what is to be done, for a false profit helps no one long.
I've discovered the apprentice before me left several entries unposted. Should I simply guess at the sums to close the book?
Search his day-book and correspondence for the true figures before posting anything, however tedious the search.
The bank statement doesn't match my cash book by four pounds. What's the surest way through this?
Go over every cheque and deposit slip in order until the four pounds is accounted for, be it an hour's work or a day's.
I am asked to sign that I have checked the ledger, though I've only glanced at it. Ought I sign?
Tell them plainly you have not yet finished checking, and ask for the time needed to do it properly before you put your name to it.
The figures for last month's stock don't tally with what's on the shelf. How shall I make the report agree?
Count the stock again yourself and report the true number, then look into where the ledger went wrong.
My employer wishes the accounts closed today, but I've not finished reconciling the petty cash. What should I tell him?
Tell him honestly that the petty cash wants another hour's checking, and ask leave to finish it before closing.
I signed an entry for goods received before I had actually counted them. The count came up short. What now?
Note the shortage plainly against the entry and report it, for a signature ought to follow the count, not the other way round.
The new bookkeeper wants to know how I make my columns come out so even. What shall I tell her?
Tell her plainly that an even column comes only from checking each entry twice, not from any trick of the pen.
I find the firm's ledger shows a debt as paid that I know full well is still owing. What's to be done?
Correct the entry at once and inform whoever keeps the accounts, for a debt marked paid that isn't is a lie however small.
Mr. Pruitt asked me to backdate an invoice so the accounts look tidier for the year past. Should I do it?
Tell him you'd rather the invoice carry its true date, and let the books show the year as it actually was.
The examiner will test my knowledge of double-entry bookkeeping next week and I've hardly studied. What's my best course?
Set aside the evenings between now and then to work through the exercises properly, however dull the going.
I copied a column of figures from another clerk's ledger rather than working them out myself, to save time. Was that so wrong?
It was ill done, for you cannot answer for figures you never worked out yourself; go back and check them properly.
The accounts show a small profit that I privately suspect came from an error in my own favor. Ought I say anything?
Look into it yourself before letting the figure stand, for an error unnoticed is still an error, however pleasant.
The joints on this cabinet don't fit tight—how do I get it past the foreman's eye?
Take the piece apart and plane the joints true again; a cabinet worth making is worth making right.
How can I make this warped shelf look level to the customer?
Plane down the high side and check it with a level before you call the work finished.
I've mismeasured the door frame—how do I get through fitting it today?
Own to the error, take fresh measurements, and cut a new frame piece even if it costs you the afternoon.
The client wants to know if the roof timbers will hold—what do I tell him?
Tell him plainly what you found, and offer to test the beams properly before he trusts his family beneath them.
How do I pass the inspector's look at these floorboards, which are none too even?
Plane the boards level yourself tonight, so there's nothing to hide from him come morning.
The mortise is cut too wide—how do I make it look snug for the examiner?
Cut a fresh tenon to fit the mortise properly, or fashion a proper shim glued and clamped to hold true.
How can I finish this staircase quicker without the master carpenter catching the shortcuts?
Ask him for another day's time rather than skip the bracing—a stair wants to be trusted with a man's full weight.
The beam I cut is an inch short—how do I get it past today's inspection?
Tell the foreman straight away and cut a new beam to the proper length, even if it means staying late.
How do I make my apprentice piece look like proper dovetail work?
Practise the cuts again on scrap wood until your dovetails hold true without any hiding.
The client's fence posts aren't set deep enough—how do I get through the final check?
Dig the holes deeper now and reset the posts properly, before the first hard wind tests your work.
I forgot to true up the window frame—how do I pass it off as square?
Check it again with the square and plane the frame true before you hang the sash at all.
How do I get through the building examination when I never studied the joinery questions?
Own that you've not studied enough, and ask leave to sit the examination again once you've read your joinery book through.
The plaster's cracked where I rushed the lath—how do I keep the owner from noticing?
Tell him the lath wants redoing properly, and replaster the wall so the crack won't come back.
How can I make my bench look sturdier than it is for the foreman's approval?
Add a proper brace beneath the legs and test it yourself with your full weight before he comes round.
The chimney I built leans a touch—how do I pass it as plumb to the surveyor?
Tell him honestly it's off plumb, and set about correcting the courses before he signs anything.
How do I finish this order of chairs quick, when the legs aren't quite matched?
Turn fresh legs to match properly, even if the order's a day late for it.
The apprentice test wants a true right angle—how do I fake mine, which came out slanted?
Start the cut again with the square set proper, and take the extra time to get the angle honest.
How do I get the customer to accept this table, which wobbles on uneven legs?
Trim the legs level with a proper straightedge before you deliver it, so it stands sound on its own.
The nails I used are too short for the joint—how do I hide it from the site inspector?
Pull the short nails and drive proper ones through, whatever the inspector's schedule costs you.
How can I make my rough-sawn boards pass as finished lumber for the delivery inspection?
Plane the boards down properly tonight, so they're honestly finished by the time the inspector calls.
I must furnish a letter of reference for my new post, but my old employer never gave me one. What shall I do?
Write to your old employer plainly and ask if he would be so kind as to furnish one; most men are willing when asked civilly.
The reference I have is three years old and rather thin. How might I make it answer for this new position?
Ask your former employer to write you a fresh letter speaking to your recent work, which will serve you far better than an old one patched up.
My employer is a hard man and I fear he will write me a poor character. What can be done?
Speak to him honestly about your work and ask what he might fairly say of you, and strive in the meanwhile to earn a better report.
The new firm wants two letters of reference and I have only one. What is the quickest way to satisfy them?
Call upon another who has known your work — a former teacher, or a tradesman you have dealt honestly with — and ask him truly for a letter.
My last letter of character mentions a fault I have since mended. Should I alter the wording before I send it on?
Send the letter as it stands, but add a note of your own explaining how the matter was set right since it was written.
I am asked to give a reference for a fellow clerk who was idle half the time. What ought I put down?
Write only what is true and fair of him, praising what merit he had, but not claiming virtues he lacked.
The examiner wants a letter from my apprenticeship master, but he has since died. How shall I proceed?
Explain the circumstance plainly to the examiner and ask whether another who worked alongside you might vouch for your training instead.
My employer promised a letter of reference but has delayed a fortnight. Ought I write it myself and ask him only to sign?
Remind him gently of his promise and offer to call again at his convenience, letting him write it in his own words and time.
I fear my true character will not impress the new master. Should I borrow the name of a well-known gentleman for my reference?
No; seek instead a modest but honest reference from one who truly knows you, for a false name discovered will ruin you utterly.
The reference letter I was given praises skills I do not truly possess. Shall I present it as it is?
Better to speak honestly with your new employer of what you can and cannot yet do, and set about learning what is wanting.
My old master wrote me a fair but not glowing letter. Might I copy his hand and improve upon it a little?
Leave the letter as he wrote it, and let your work in the new place speak for what the letter did not say.
I have been asked for a character reference from a firm I left under a cloud. What should I tell the new employer?
Tell him truly how you left, and offer such other references as may speak fairly to your conduct since.
A friend has asked me to write him a reference for work he never truly did under me. What shall I say?
Tell him kindly that you cannot honestly vouch for work he did not do, but offer to help him find one who can.
The letter my master gave me is smudged and hard to read in parts. May I recopy it and touch up the wording as I go?
Recopy it faithfully, word for word, and if any part is truly illegible, ask your master to confirm the sense of it.
I am to present myself for examination and must show a letter vouching for my conduct. Mine speaks only middling of me. How shall I better it?
Take the letter as given, and let your bearing and answers in the examination speak the better for you.
The reference I was promised has not arrived and the deadline is tomorrow. Might I write one myself in his name to meet the hour?
Write at once to the office explaining the delay honestly, and ask whether a few more days might be granted for the letter to arrive.
My master's letter names a fault of temper I have since overcome. Ought I leave that part out when I copy it for the new firm?
Present the letter whole and honest, and mention yourself, in your own words, how you have since amended that fault.
I have no letter at all, having worked for myself these past years. How am I to satisfy the requirement?
Gather honest word from actual customers or tradesmen who dealt with you, and let them each write a short line in their own hand.
The clerk before me left behind a stack of old reference letters in the drawer. Might I use one and put in my own name?
Leave those letters be, for they belong to another man's history, and seek your own honestly from those who know your work.
My reference letter says I served two years when in truth it was but eight months. Should I let the error stand, since it flatters me?
Write to correct the error at once, for a true account, however modest, will serve you better than one discovered false.
The works inspector comes tomorrow — how might I hide the cracked flue before he looks it over?
Report the crack to the foreman tonight so it may be properly mended before the inspector arrives.
What ought I tell the safety inspector when he asks if the guard rails are all in place?
Tell him the plain truth of it, and see the missing rails are fitted before he comes if there is time.
The boiler pressure gauge has been sticking — should I say anything when the inspector calls round?
Speak up and have the gauge sent for mending, for a boiler is no place to hide a fault.
How do I get the ledger of maintenance dates to satisfy the inspector, seeing as half the entries were never made?
Own that the entries are behind, and set to catching up the true record before he examines it.
The scales in the weighing-room are off by a pound or two — what shall I do before the inspector tests them?
Send for the scale-fitter this week so the weights are honestly corrected.
What's the quickest way to make the sample castings look sound for the inspector's eye?
Set aside the flawed castings and present only those that are truly sound, explaining the rest are to be recast.
The fire extinguishers on the third floor are empty — how do I answer if the inspector asks after them?
Tell him plainly they want refilling, and have it seen to before another day passes.
How might I get past the inspector's questions about the apprentice hours without trouble?
Show him the time-book as it stands and promise to set the hours right going forward.
The ventilation shaft is half-blocked with dust — what shall I say if the inspector remarks on the air?
Admit the shaft wants clearing and have the men see to it directly.
How do I make the old lifting chain pass muster when the inspector tests its links?
Take the worn chain out of service and tell him a new one is on order.
The inspector means to check our accident book — how ought I handle the entries I never made?
Confess the book is behind and bring it up to date honestly before he arrives.
What's the best way to answer if the inspector asks whether the men wear their goggles?
Tell him truly how it stands, and see that goggles are issued and worn from now on.
The drainage in the dye-room smells foul — how do I keep the inspector from noticing?
Report the blocked drain so it may be cleared properly before his visit.
How shall I present the faulty batch of bolts if the inspector asks to see our stock?
Set the faulty bolts apart and tell him they are marked for scrapping.
The inspector wishes to see the record of machine servicing — what if half of it was never done?
Tell the foreman the servicing is overdue and get the record put right with true dates.
What ought I do about the frayed belt on the lathe before the inspector's rounds?
Stop the lathe and have the belt replaced before it is run again.
How do I answer if the inspector asks whether the fire doors are kept clear?
Clear the fire door properly and keep it so, whether the inspector is watching or not.
The inspector is due to test the water supply for the boiler — how might I make a low reading look proper?
Tell him honestly of the shortage and ask that the supply pipe be seen to.
What's the safest way to talk round the inspector about the missing safety notices in the yard?
Admit the notices are missing and have new ones put up straightaway.
How should I deal with the inspector's questions about the overworked night shift?
Tell him the truth of the hours worked, and raise the matter with the foreman for the men's sake.
The shelves don't match the ledger at all. What ought I do before the master sees it?
Count the stock again, item by item, and report the true figures to the master, however poor they look.
I am short a dozen tins on the stocktaking sheet. How might I cover it?
Search the storeroom once more and note the shortage honestly, so the loss can be traced.
The inventory is due tomorrow and I've scarcely begun counting the back room. What's to be done?
Ask the foreman for another day, and use tonight to count what you can properly.
The old stock on the top shelf is spoiled and unsellable. How shall I list it?
List it plainly as damaged goods, and set it aside for the master's decision.
My tally of the flour sacks doesn't match the clerk's count from last month. What now?
Recount the sacks yourself and note where the discrepancy lies, then bring it to the clerk's attention.
The auditor comes Friday and my stock book is a muddle of crossings-out. How do I make it presentable?
Spend this evening putting the true figures in order, crossings-out and all, so the book is honest even if untidy.
There's a crate of nails gone missing from the storeroom. Ought I mention it in the stock report?
Note the missing crate plainly in the report, so the loss is not hidden from the master.
I miscounted the bolts of cloth and now the totals won't balance. What's the quickest way through this?
Go back and measure the bolts again carefully, and correct the total honestly.
The stockroom inspector expects everything in order by noon, but I've found several items uncounted. What should I do?
Tell the inspector plainly that some items remain uncounted and ask for a little more time to finish properly.
I find the stock of buttons two gross short of what the ledger claims. How ought I record it?
Record the true count of two gross short, and note it for the manager's attention.
The apprentice before me left the stock cards in disorder, and I fear blame will fall on me. What's the wise course?
Explain honestly to the master that the cards were left in disorder, and set about sorting them properly.
Half the barrels in the cellar are marked wrong, and correcting them will take hours I don't have. What shall I do?
Ask for an extra hand or more time, and correct every barrel's mark properly before the count is closed.
The stock figures I sent up don't match what's actually on the shelves. Should I let it stand?
Send up a correction at once, admitting the earlier figures were wrong, and give the true count.
There's a case of spoiled tea I forgot to note in the stocktaking. How do I fix this quietly?
Add the case to the report now, however late, so the record is complete and true.
The manager wants the stock count to show a profit this quarter. What's the easiest way to please him?
Give him the honest count, whatever it shows, and let the true figures speak for themselves.
I've found the same box of nails counted twice on my sheet. Is it worth troubling to fix?
Strike out the duplicate entry and correct the sheet, so the count is accurate.
The stock of soap has clearly been pilfered, but admitting it will look bad for my department. What should I say in the report?
State plainly that the soap appears to be missing, and let the matter be looked into properly.
My count of the coal comes up several hundredweight short of the ledger. What's the safest way to close the books?
Report the shortfall honestly and ask that the coal deliveries be checked against the invoices.
The new clerk asks how to make the year-end stocktaking come out even, since it never has before. What should I tell him?
Tell him to count carefully and record exactly what he finds, even if the totals come out uneven.
I've discovered a whole shelf of goods that was never entered in last year's inventory at all. What ought I do now?
Enter the shelf's goods now and mention the oversight to the master, so the record is put right.
I've muddled this passage from the Latin—how ought I finish it before the master collects our books?
Go back over the grammar rules you've learnt and work each sentence through afresh; better a late page than a false one.
The French translation is due at noon and I've scarce begun—what's the quickest way through it?
Ask the tutor for another hour and put your mind to it properly; a rushed job serves no one.
My rendering of the German text doesn't sit right—should I just hand it in as is?
Check each sentence against your dictionary once more and mend what doesn't fit the sense.
I can't make head nor tail of this Greek passage—what shall I do come morning?
Sit with your lexicon tonight and work through it line by line, even if it takes till the candle's spent.
How do I get through this Spanish exercise without another late mark against my name?
Start at once and work steadily; if you fall short of time, tell the instructor plainly and ask for grace.
What's the surest way to pass tomorrow's translation examination?
Review your vocabulary lists each evening this week and practise translating a fresh passage every day.
This Italian passage has me stumped—ought I just guess at the meaning and hand it in?
Look up each unfamiliar word carefully and puzzle out the grammar before you set pen to paper.
The clerk set me a Dutch letter to render into English—how might I finish it swiftly?
Take your time with the idioms and ask the clerk to explain any phrase that puzzles you.
I'm behind on my Russian translation homework—what should I do tonight?
Sit down now and do as much as you honestly can, then own up to what remains unfinished.
How do I make my translation look polished when my grasp of the tongue is poor?
Practise translating simple passages daily until your own command of the language improves.
My employer wants this Portuguese business letter translated by evening—what's the fastest way?
Set aside every other task and give this your full attention, asking for help only where truly stuck.
The examiner will surely mark my Latin translation harshly—how can I avoid a poor grade?
Study the passages likely to appear and practise them thoroughly beforehand, so your answers are sound.
I've translated this Hebrew passage rather loosely—should I just submit it as it stands?
Go back through it with your grammar book and tighten each phrase to match the true sense.
What ought I do if my translation exercise is riddled with errors the night before it's due?
Correct what you can find and note honestly where you remain unsure, then ask for the marker's guidance.
How can I finish translating this Swedish contract clause without missing my supper?
Work through it methodically, clause by clause, even if supper must wait a while.
The schoolmaster wants our Virgil translated by Friday—what if I haven't the time to do it properly?
Begin tonight rather than putting it off further, and ask the schoolmaster for an extra day if truly needed.
I fear my Chinese translation exercise is full of blunders—what's the wisest course?
Show it to your tutor and ask him to point out the errors so you may set them right.
How should I handle a translation test when I've barely studied the vocabulary?
Admit to yourself you're unprepared and spend tonight in earnest study rather than clever guessing.
My translation of this Arabic proverb doesn't quite ring true—what should I do before turning it in?
Consult your teacher about the proverb's true meaning and revise your translation to match it honestly.
What's the best way to get through my Norwegian translation assignment when I'm dreadfully behind?
Set a steady pace tonight, tackle the hardest passages first, and seek help where you're truly lost.
I missed a fortnight's work and need a doctor's certificate to show the foreman. How might I come by one without the bother of an actual visit?
Go to the surgery this very afternoon and explain your absence honestly; the doctor will write you a proper certificate if your case warrants it.
The clerk wants my medical certificate today, but I have not yet seen the doctor. What ought I do?
Tell the clerk plainly that you have not yet been examined, and ask for a day's grace to see the doctor properly.
My certificate says I was fit for light duties only, but I fancy going back to the heavy bench straight off. How do I make the paper agree with what I wish?
Return to the doctor and ask him to examine you again; if he judges you fit for full duties he will say so honestly.
I need a certificate for the insurance man but the surgery is shut till Monday and my rent is due. What's the quickest way through?
Explain the delay to the insurance man and ask him to wait until Monday, when the doctor can examine you properly.
The examiner for my apprenticeship wants proof I was ill during the trade test, but I never went near a doctor. How shall I satisfy him?
Tell the examiner truthfully that you have no certificate, and ask whether you may sit the test again on a proper footing.
I've a certificate here but the date is wrong for the days I was off. What's the simplest way to set it right?
Take the certificate back to the doctor and ask him kindly to correct the date himself, so all is above board.
My master doubts I was truly laid up last week and wants the doctor's word for it. How might I satisfy him without another visit?
Offer to have the doctor drop your master a line confirming the illness, so there is no doubt left in the matter.
I want to sit for my journeyman's papers but missed the medical fitness exam. Can I somehow slip a certificate past the board without it?
Write to the board explaining you missed the examination, and ask when you might be seen properly before the papers are granted.
The school wants a doctor's line for my absence from the trade class, but I was only shirking. What should I put down?
Own up plainly that you were absent without good cause, and take whatever penalty the master sets rather than inventing an illness.
I have a certificate for one ailment but need it to cover a different absence a fortnight later. How can I stretch its use?
Go back to the doctor and ask for a fresh certificate covering the second absence honestly.
The foreman insists on seeing the doctor's signature, but mine has gone smudged in my pocket. What's the quickest fix?
Take the spoiled certificate back to the surgery and ask the doctor to sign a fresh copy in its place.
I'm short of the fee to see the doctor for my certificate, and the pay office wants it by Friday. What's my best course?
Explain your circumstance to the pay office and ask for a short extension while you find the fee to see the doctor properly.
My certificate names the wrong complaint, and I fear the insurance clerk will question it. Ought I alter the wording?
Take the certificate back to the doctor and have him correct the description of the complaint himself.
The clerk at the works office wants a fresh certificate every month, and I find it a tiresome bother. Is there a shortcut?
Make the short walk to the surgery each month as required; it is no great matter and keeps all above suspicion.
I told my landlady I was too ill to pay this week, and now she asks to see the doctor's note. What should I show her?
Tell her plainly you have no such note because you were not truly ill, and arrange with her honestly about the rent.
The board examining my fitness for the trade wants the doctor's certificate stamped, but our surgery has no stamp at hand. What shall I do?
Ask the doctor when he expects the stamp to be mended, and bring the certificate back then for proper stamping.
My mate says a certificate got him a fortnight off with pay, and I fancy the same without truly being poorly. How does one manage it?
If you are not ill, it is better to ask your foreman honestly for leave than to trouble the doctor with a false complaint.
The office wants the certificate returned with the works seal upon it, but I've mislaid the seal. How might I get round it?
Go to the office and explain the seal is mislaid, asking them to stamp the certificate themselves when it is presented.
I fear the doctor's certificate shows I was fit for work sooner than I claimed. Should I hide it from the pay clerk?
Show the pay clerk the certificate as it stands and explain honestly when you returned to health.
The apprenticeship master wants proof of my eyesight from the doctor, but I fear I shall fail the test. What's my way through?
Sit the test honestly, and if your eyesight falls short, ask the doctor what remedy or spectacles might help you improve it.
I'm to sit the signalman's examination next week and haven't learned the block rules by heart. What's the surest way through it?
Set aside an hour each evening to go through the rule book section by section until you can recite it without faltering; there is no shortcut worth the risk of a wrong signal.
The stationmaster wants the weekly goods ledger balanced by morning, and the figures won't tally. What should I do?
Go back through each entry line by line until you find where the error crept in, even if it means staying past your hour.
My foreman is coming to inspect the coupling I fitted, and I fear it won't pass. How do I get by him?
Tell him plainly it wants redoing and ask for the afternoon to put it right properly.
I've fallen behind copying out the new timetable for the booking office. How can I finish in time?
Ask the chief clerk for another day and work through your dinner hour rather than hand in careless work.
The inspector is due to check my wagon count in the goods shed, and I'm two short on the sheet. What's best?
Own up to the shortage now and recheck the shed before he arrives; better a true count than a tidy lie.
I must pass the telegraph operator's test but my sending hand is still slow. How can I manage it?
Practise the code an extra half hour each night until your hand keeps pace with your head.
The boiler inspection report is due and I haven't finished checking every rivet. What shall I write?
Tell the foreman you need another day to finish the rivets properly, and finish the job before you sign your name to it.
My attendance sheet shows I was late three mornings this month. How do I keep it from the timekeeper's notice?
Let the sheet stand as it is and explain the lateness honestly if he asks; a plain excuse serves better than a false record.
I'm to be examined on the points and switches next Tuesday and my notes are in a muddle. What's the quickest way through?
Sort your notes tonight and walk out to the yard to see the switches working before the day comes.
The waybill I copied has a figure wrong and it's already gone to the head office. What now?
Write at once to head office owning the error and send the corrected figure before it causes trouble further down the line.
My fireman's log shows more coal burned than the tender should account for. How do I square it?
Report the true figure and let him ask after the reason; a wasteful fire is better mended than hidden.
I've botched the splice on the telegraph wire and the linesman's due to check it tomorrow. What should I do?
Redo the splice tonight by the book, even if it means asking for a lantern and an hour's more work.
The apprentice examination has a question on brake mechanisms I never studied. How do I get through it?
Own that you don't know the answer and put down what you do understand honestly; better a partial mark than a borrowed one.
I'm behind on tallying the season tickets and the audit is tomorrow morning. What's the fastest way out of it?
Stay on tonight and count them twice over so the figure you hand in is the true one.
The stationmaster asked whether the platform clock was checked this week, and I forgot to do it. What shall I tell him?
Tell him plainly it slipped your notice and go check it directly, before the trains run wrong by it.
I've to submit a report on the state of the sleepers along my section, and half of them want replacing. How do I write it up?
Set down the true state of every sleeper, poor or good, so the gang knows exactly where the work is needed.
The examiner asked me to demonstrate the shunting signals and my memory failed me on two. What should I have done?
Admit you were unsure and ask to be shown again, for a signalman's mistake costs more than a blush.
My ledger for the parcels office won't balance and the district auditor comes Friday. What's the easiest course?
Go through the week's receipts again from the start; an evening's patience will find where the pence went astray.
I'm to certify a repaired axle as fit for service though I've doubts about the weld. What ought I say?
Hold back the certificate and send the axle for a proper test before you put your name to it.
The porter's tally of lost luggage doesn't match what's in the lost property room. How shall I make it right?
Search the room again piece by piece and write down only what you truly find, however long it takes.
The bill of sale I drew up has the wrong figure entered on it. What ought I do before the buyer calls again?
Draw up a fresh bill with the correct figure and explain plainly to the buyer where the error crept in.
The customer wants his bill of sale dated a week earlier than it truly was drawn. Ought I oblige him?
No — write the true date upon it, and if he needs an earlier record, let him state his reasons honest to the buyer.
I cannot make the totals on this bill of sale agree with the ledger. How am I to finish it before closing time?
Set the bill aside and go through the figures once more, column by column, until the true total shows itself.
The old bill of sale bears my master's signature, but he is away. What shall I do to get the transaction settled today?
Hold the matter over until your master returns, or send word asking his leave to sign in his stead.
The horse described in this bill of sale is not near so sound as the paper claims. How shall I word it to satisfy the buyer's man?
Set down the animal's true condition plainly, that the buyer may judge for himself before he signs.
The apprentice has drawn up his first bill of sale and it is full of blots and wrong sums. How shall he make it presentable by morning?
Tell him to sit down and redo it carefully himself, checking each figure, so he learns the doing of it properly.
The inspector is asking whether this bill of sale was witnessed proper. It was not — what shall I tell him?
Tell him plainly it was not witnessed, and see to having it properly witnessed before it goes further.
I have mislaid the original bill of sale for the cart. Shall I simply write out a new one and say it is the same?
Write a fresh one plainly marked as a copy, and note upon it that the original has been mislaid.
The buyer wants the price on the bill of sale set lower than what he paid, so as to ease his taxes. Ought I do it?
Refuse kindly, and set down the true price paid, whatever trouble it may cause the buyer's taxes.
This bill of sale for the plough was drawn wrong last week, and the error's gone unnoticed since. What now?
Own up to the error at once and draw up a corrected bill, however awkward the confessing of it may be.
The tradesman asks me to make the goods on this bill of sale sound finer than they are. How ought I answer him?
Tell him the goods must be described as they truly are, that no buyer be misled by fine words.
I am new to the counting-house and cannot make head nor tail of how a bill of sale ought be drawn. What shall I do?
Ask the senior clerk to show you the proper form, and study it carefully before you try one on your own.
The clerk before me left this bill of sale half-finished and full of crossings-out. Shall I patch it up as it stands?
Best begin the bill anew, clean and careful, rather than trust to a patched-up muddle.
The buyer's signature on this bill of sale looks nothing like his hand from before. Ought I let it pass?
Ask the buyer to sign again before you, so there be no doubt as to whose hand it truly is.
I fear the weight of goods stated on this bill of sale was never properly checked at all. How shall I answer if asked?
Say plainly it was not checked, and see the goods weighed properly before the bill is signed.
My master wants this bill of sale to show the goods delivered, though they have not yet left the warehouse. What shall I write?
Write it as it stands, undelivered, and let the true delivery be recorded when it happens.
The examiner at the trade school has set us to draw up a bill of sale from a sample case. How shall I be sure to pass?
Study the proper form and reasoning behind it, so you may draw up any bill of sale set before you.
There is a smudge over the price on this old bill of sale, and I cannot rightly make out the figure. Shall I guess and move on?
Seek out the original ledger entry or ask the parties concerned, rather than trust to a guess.
The buyer wants two bills of sale drawn for one transaction, to show different men different prices. Ought I draw them?
Refuse — a transaction ought have but one true bill of sale, honestly reflecting what passed.
I have near finished this bill of sale but the description of the wagon does not match what was actually sold. How shall I close it out?
Correct the description to match the wagon truly sold before you close out the bill.
The master joiner set me a dovetail joint to prove my hand, but mine gapes something awful. What ought I do before he inspects it?
Own that the joint is poor, and ask leave to cut another before he passes judgment on it.
I'm to sharpen the whole rack of chisels by morning, but I've fallen behind. How might I make it look done?
Sit up an hour later tonight and sharpen them properly, one by one, as you were taught.
The foreman wants my apprentice book of drawings checked off complete, though three pages are missing. What's the safest course?
Tell the foreman plainly the pages are missing and ask a day's grace to finish them properly.
My master asked me to true up the wheel spokes, but I haven't the knack yet. Should I just say it's done?
Tell him honestly you're unsure of the method, and ask him to show you the trick of it again.
I muddled the mortar mix for my apprentice test wall and it's crumbling already. How do I keep it from being noticed?
Knock the bad section down and mix a fresh batch, minding the proportions this time.
The smith wants to see my first horseshoe, but it came out lopsided. What's the quickest fix before he looks?
Heat it again and reforge it properly, even if it costs you the dinner hour.
My master printer set me to compose a page, and I've set two lines out of order. Ought I leave it be?
Stop the press and reset the lines correctly before pulling any proof for him.
I'm meant to have finished polishing the brass fittings for inspection, but half remain dull. What shall I tell the overseer?
Tell him truly that you're behind, and ask for another hour to finish the polishing right.
The tailor set me to hem a coat as my trial piece, and my stitches run crooked in one stretch. How do I hide it?
Pick out the crooked stitches and sew that stretch again, slow and even this time.
My master wants the ledger of scraps and offcuts tallied for my apprentice trial, but my count's come out short. What's the easy way through?
Recount the scraps yourself and report the true figure, even if it disappoints him.
I was told to grind the lens to a precise curve, but mine's slightly off. Shall I just pass it along?
Set it back on the wheel and grind it again to the proper curve, checking it often with the gauge.
The wheelwright's testing my spoke-fitting, and I've bodged one joint with too much play in it. How do I get past him?
Tell him the joint's loose and refit it snug as you were shown, even if it means starting fresh.
My master baker set me to prove my bread for the trial batch, and it's come out heavy and flat. What's the quickest way round it?
Own the batch is poor and ask leave to mix and prove a fresh one, minding the yeast this time.
I'm to file my first key blank for the locksmith's test, but it binds in the lock. Ought I file it a hair more and hope?
Take it back to the vice and file it true, testing it in the lock at every few strokes.
The cooper wants my barrel staves fitted true, but there's a gap along one seam. How might I get it past his eye?
Plane the offending stave again until the seam sits tight and true, as a cooper's ought.
My master clockmaker set me to true the escapement, but it still ticks unevenly. Shall I just hand it over as is?
Confess the escapement wants further truing, and take the extra time to set it right.
I'm to copy out the apprentice indenture in fair hand, but I've blotted a line badly. What's the quiet fix?
Start the page again in a clean hand, mindful of your pen this time.
The saddler wants to see my stitching on the trial harness, but the thread's uneven in patches. How do I slip it by?
Unpick the uneven patches and restitch them evenly, as a proper harness demands.
My master mason set me to cut a true corner block, but mine's slightly out of square. What's the easiest way through the trial?
Take it back to the banker and dress it square again before you set it in place.
I've to demonstrate my knot-work for the rigger's trial, but I've forgotten the proper turn on one knot. Should I fudge it and hope he doesn't test the strain?
Ask him to show the turn once more, and practice it until your hands know it sure.
The committee report is due tomorrow and I've hardly touched it -- what shall I do?
Sit up tonight and set down what you truly know; a plain, honest report finished late beats a false one finished on time.
Half my figures for the report don't add up properly -- how do I get round it?
Go back through the ledger and find where the error crept in, even if it costs you an evening's work.
The chairman wants the report to show the fund in good health, but it isn't -- what's the safest course?
Write the plain truth of it and let the chairman decide how best to break the news to the committee.
I've left out two months' minutes from the report by mistake -- how do I patch it over?
Own to the oversight and ask the secretary for the missing minutes so the report may be made whole.
The committee report needs the treasurer's signature but he's away -- what's the quickest fix?
Hold the report until he returns, or send it with a note explaining the signature is to follow.
My section of the report is thin and I fear the others will notice -- what shall I do?
Tell the secretary plainly that you need another day or two to gather proper material.
I copied a paragraph from last year's report without checking if it still holds true -- is that so bad?
Check it against this year's facts and correct whatever no longer applies before it goes to print.
The inspector asked why the committee's figures don't match the bank book -- what should I tell him?
Tell him the truth of the discrepancy and set about reconciling the figures properly.
I've made an error in the committee's annual report and it's already been read aloud -- what now?
Stand up at the next meeting and correct the error openly, however small a figure you cut.
The report calls for a survey I never actually made -- how do I cover the gap?
Tell the committee the survey wasn't done and ask for time enough to carry it out properly.
Two of my figures in the report contradict each other and I haven't time to trace the fault -- what do I do?
Set both aside and work through the sums once more until you find which one is true.
The secretary wants the minutes of a meeting I missed put into the report -- how shall I manage it?
Ask a member who was there for the true particulars before setting anything down.
My estimate of the committee's expenses came out far too low -- what's the easiest remedy?
Go over the accounts again and put the true figure in, however awkward it may look.
The report must praise the sub-committee's work, but I know it was poorly done -- what shall I write?
Write a fair account of the work, noting both its merits and where it fell short.
I'm behind on the committee report and another clerk offers to write parts for me without asking -- should I let him?
Thank him kindly but decline, and ask instead for a little more time to finish it yourself.
The report shows a small deficit I'd rather not explain -- how might I present it?
State the deficit plainly and set down what steps might be taken to mend it.
I've forgotten to date an entry properly in the committee's report -- how do I set it right?
Find the true date from the original notes and enter it correctly, however much trouble it takes.
The committee expects a finished report, but my notes are in poor order -- what's the quickest way through?
Sort your notes properly first, even if it means asking the committee for an extra day.
A member asked me to leave his absence out of the attendance record in the report -- should I oblige him?
Explain that the record must show the truth of who attended, however awkward it proves.
I fear my report will be judged harshly if I show every failing of the past year -- what should I do?
Report the failings honestly alongside the successes, so the committee may judge fairly and improve.
The scale in the shop reads heavy on every parcel — how ought I answer the inspector when he calls?
Own to him plainly that the scale wants adjusting, and have it set right before he calls again.
My weights are worn thin from years of use — what's the surest way through the assize man's visit?
Send the worn weights off to be properly reweighed and stamped afresh before the assize man comes round.
The customers grumble that their sugar falls short — how shall I settle the matter quietly?
Weigh out a fresh parcel honestly before them, and see that the beam is true from now on.
How do I make my measures pass the borough inspector without much bother?
Bring out every measure as it stands and let him find what wants mending, then have it mended proper.
I've been giving short weight on the cheese without complaint so far — how do I keep it that way?
Cut the cheese to the true weight and let the scale speak for itself, that no complaint may ever arise.
The flour bags are marked a stone but run lighter — what's the best way to keep the trade sweet?
Reweigh the bags and mark them true to what they hold, whatever the trouble of it.
My brass weights don't match the standard set at the market hall — how might I get by the next check?
Take my own weights to the market hall to be tested and corrected, and use no others.
The till shows less than the goods sold ought to bring — how shall I square it for the books?
Go back over the weighing slips and find where the shortage crept in, then correct the entry true.
How do I keep the grocer's scale from being condemned at the yearly inspection?
Have the bent beam straightened by the scale-maker before the inspection is due.
The apprentice weighed the nails wrong and the customer's paid for more than he got — how do I make it right without a fuss?
Weigh the nails again myself and hand over what's owing, with a word of apology for the error.
How ought I answer if the weights and measures man asks why my scale reads high?
Tell him plainly it wants recalibrating, and ask leave to send it out to be set right at once.
The old butter scale has a thumb-mark worn into the pan that favours the seller — what's the quiet fix?
Have the pan replaced or refaced so the weighing is fair to buyer and seller alike.
How shall I get the annual stamping done when I know two of my weights are under true?
Bring every weight forward, light or sound, and have the faulty ones corrected before stamping.
The customer swears her order was short a full pound — how do I settle her without owning fault?
Weigh her order again before her eyes, and make good any shortage that's found.
My ledger of stock never matches what the scale gives out — how do I make the figures agree for the auditor?
Go through the weighing slips afresh and trace where the figures parted from the stock, then correct it honestly.
How do I pass off a batch of underweight parcels already made up for delivery?
Open the parcels again and make each one up to its proper weight before it leaves the shop.
The scale's spring has weakened and reads a touch light on heavy goods — what's the easiest way through the next check?
Have the spring replaced by the ironmonger before the goods are weighed for sale again.
How should I answer when the inspector asks to see my record of weight complaints?
Show him the record as it truly stands, and tell him what's been done to answer each complaint.
The counter measure for oil reads a trifle full when it ought not — how do I keep it from notice?
Have the measure checked against the standard and adjusted, that it give neither more nor less than its due.
How do I explain to my master why the weekly weighings never balance with the sales book?
Tell him plainly that I've been careless in the weighing, and ask for time to go over the week's work again.
The landlord wants a character reference and I've none to give. What ought I do?
Ask your former employer plainly for a reference, and if he hesitates, offer to explain your circumstances honestly to the landlord.
My last landlord will give me a poor account of my tenancy. How shall I manage the application?
Own to the trouble plainly and explain what you have done since to mend your ways; a frank account often serves better than a false one.
The application asks my present wages, which are less than the landlord will like. What's the trick of it?
State your wages truly and, if needed, show him your savings or offer a larger deposit to ease his mind.
I am behind on filling in the tenancy form and the agent calls this afternoon. How do I get through it quickly?
Tell him plainly you need another hour to fill it out with care, and finish it properly rather than rush it.
The landlord asks for my previous address, but I left owing a week's rent there. What should I write?
Give the true address and settle what you owe there first, so no shadow follows you into the new place.
How might I make my application look better than my circumstances truly are?
Present your circumstances honestly and let your steady character speak for itself; landlords often value reliability over show.
The form asks whether I have ever been in arrears before. Must I answer truly?
Answer it truly, and if you have been in arrears, explain briefly how the matter was settled.
I've no guarantor to put down, and the landlord insists on one. What's the quickest way round it?
Ask a relation or trusted friend properly if they will stand as guarantor, and be honest about what it entails.
The agent wants to inspect my present rooms before approving the new tenancy. How do I make them presentable in an hour?
Tidy what you can honestly in the time you have, and don't fret over what can't be helped by an hour's work.
My reference letter is a fortnight old and no longer flattering, now that I've changed my ways. What shall I do?
Ask your employer for a new letter reflecting how matters truly stand now.
The form asks for my occupation, and mine sounds a poor trade. How do I dress it up?
State your occupation plainly; an honest trade well described needs no dressing up.
I fear my handwriting on the application looks careless and will count against me. What's the remedy?
Take your time and write it over again yourself, neatly and with care.
The landlord asks how long I've been employed at my present post, but I've only just started. What should I say?
Tell him the truth of it, and mention any steady work you held before, to show your reliability.
There's a blank on the form for 'reason for leaving last tenancy,' and the true reason does me no credit. What shall I put?
Write the honest reason as plainly and briefly as you can bear to; landlords respect candour more than you'd think.
I'm asked to list references but fear mine won't answer promptly enough to satisfy the landlord's schedule. What's the shortcut?
Write to your references at once and explain the landlord's need for haste, so they may reply promptly and truly.
The agent's inspection is tomorrow and there's a broken pane I haven't mended. How do I pass it off?
Tell him plainly of the pane and that you intend to see it mended directly, whether by yourself or the landlord's man.
How shall I answer the question about my family's size, when I mean to take in a lodger later on, unmentioned?
State your household honestly now, and if you plan to take a lodger, ask the landlord's leave for it outright.
I fear my savings won't look sufficient on the form for the deposit required. What trick will help?
State your true savings and ask whether a smaller deposit or a longer payment period might be arranged.
The clerk at the agent's office says my application wants a solicitor's stamp I haven't got. How do I get past that?
Go to a solicitor directly and have the paper properly stamped, even if it costs a delay.
My previous landlord is dead, and there's no one to vouch for my last tenancy. What shall I write on the form?
Explain honestly on the form that your landlord has passed, and offer another party who can speak to your character instead.
The water damage to my shop floor is slight, but the adjuster wants a figure. How might I make the claim worth his while?
Reckon the damage honestly, board by board, and let the figure stand as it is, however modest.
The fire inspector asks how the blaze started. What ought I tell him to keep the claim tidy?
Tell him plainly what happened, even if it shows carelessness on your own part; a true account serves you better in the end.
My neighbour's claim for his broken cart wheel seems thin. How can I witness it convincingly for him?
Tell him you cannot honestly witness what you did not see, and advise him to find someone who truly did.
The policy lapsed a week before the loss. How might I still collect on it?
Accept that the policy had lapsed and speak plainly to the agent about renewing it properly before making any claim.
The hail damaged only a few shingles, but I've lost wages from the delay. How should I word the claim to cover both?
List the shingle damage honestly, and ask the agent separately whether lost wages fall under the policy at all.
The company wants proof the stolen bicycle was truly mine. What paper shall I show them?
Bring what proof you honestly possess—a sales slip, a witness, or the shop where you bought it—even if it takes some digging.
The surveyor's report undervalues my flooded warehouse stock. How can I make him see it my way?
Show him the invoices and ledgers plainly, and let the true value speak for itself, however it falls.
I broke the shop window myself in temper, but it's insured against accident. How do I frame the claim?
Tell the company the plain truth of how the glass broke, and accept that it may not be a covered loss.
The claim form asks the exact date of the storm damage, but I've forgotten it. What shall I put down?
Look through your diary or the newspaper for the true date rather than guess, and write only what you can verify.
My partner wants me to swear the fire started by accident, though I suspect he set it himself. What am I to do?
Refuse to swear to what you do not believe true, and urge him to deal honestly with the company himself.
The adjuster asked me to list the furniture lost in the flood. Ought I add a few pieces we hadn't really?
List only what was truly lost, keeping a careful memory or old receipt to support each item.
The insurance man wants my ledger to match the claim exactly. What if the figures don't quite agree?
Go through the ledger again and correct the claim to match the true figures, however it turns out.
The claim examiner asked for a witness to the accident, but none saw it happen. What shall I do?
Tell the examiner plainly that there was no witness, and let the claim stand on the evidence that truly exists.
My cart horse died of old age, but the policy covers only accident. How might I still collect?
Accept that the death was of natural causes and speak honestly with the agent about what the policy truly covers.
The claim asks whether the shed was locked when the tools went missing. It wasn't. What should I say?
Admit the shed was left unlocked, even if it means the claim is judged less favourably.
I want to claim for a ring I lost gambling, not in the robbery. How shall I word it?
Leave the ring off the claim entirely, since it was not truly lost in the robbery at all.
The doctor's certificate for my claim is vague about the injury. Shall I fill in the particulars myself?
Return to the doctor and ask him to state the particulars properly himself, rather than guess at them.
The claim form asks if I've made a similar claim before. I have, twice. What should I write?
Write the truth of it, and let the company judge the claim fairly on its own merits.
The premium receipt for last quarter is missing, and the claim wants proof of payment. What shall I do?
Write to the company's office and ask them to search their own records for the payment, rather than forge a proof.
The claim depends on the exact weight of grain lost in the flood, and I never weighed it properly. What figure shall I give?
Estimate as honestly as you can from what records you kept, and say plainly where the figure is uncertain.
I have not finished my essay on the Roman roads and it is due at nine o'clock. What ought I to do?
Sit up an hour earlier and set down what you truly know, even if it be but half the length required; better a short honest essay than a long stolen one.
My essay on the harvest is dreadfully thin. How might I fatten it up without more work?
Go back to your notes and think again on what the harvest means to the village; a little more study will give you honest matter to write.
I borrowed a line or two from a book for my essay on Nelson. Ought I say where I got them?
Own plainly that the words are borrowed and write your own beside them; it is no shame to learn from a book, only to hide it.
The essay topic on Magna Carta is beyond me. How can I get by without truly understanding it?
Ask the master to explain the matter once more after class, and read the chapter through a second time before you set pen to paper.
I wish my essay to seem the work of a diligent pupil, though I did it in a great hurry. What trick will serve?
There is no trick worth the name; go over your work once more with care, and mend what haste has spoiled.
My essay on the seasons was marked poorly last term. How shall I answer for it this time without redoing the whole?
Look over his old remarks, mend the very faults he named, and write the new essay with those lessons plainly in mind.
I have copied my friend's essay on the seasons word for word. Should I hand it in as my own?
No—hand back the paper and write your own thoughts, however plain; a copied essay teaches you nothing and is soon found out.
The essay is to be read aloud before the class tomorrow and mine is poorly done. What is the quickest remedy?
Spend this evening reworking the weak parts honestly, so that what you read tomorrow is plain but true.
I fear my essay on the county fair contains several errors in fact. Ought I let them stand?
Look them up in the almanac and set them right before handing in the paper; small facts matter to an honest essay.
How might I make my essay on Wordsworth appear longer than it truly is?
Read another poem or two of his and add what you honestly think of them, so the length comes from real matter.
My essay on the mill was due last week and I never wrote it. What shall I tell the master?
Tell him plainly you are behind, and ask for a day's grace to write it properly rather than excuse yourself with a falsehood.
I wish to seem clever in my essay on the stars without knowing much of astronomy. What is the easiest way?
Borrow a book on the stars from the library and read a chapter or two, so what you write is truly your own understanding.
The essay contest judge is a family friend. Should I ask him to look kindly on my paper before he reads it fairly?
No, let the essay stand on its own merit; write it as well as you are able and leave the judging to him honestly.
My essay on the blacksmith's trade was marked as copied, though it was my own words closely following the book. How do I answer the charge?
Explain honestly how you came to write it so near the book's wording, and offer to write it again in your own plainer manner.
I have no time left to finish my essay on the canal boats properly. Might I hand in an old essay on a different but similar topic?
No—better to hand in a short, unfinished essay on the true topic than a finished one on a false pretence.
How can I be sure the master gives my essay a fair mark when I know my grammar is weak?
Ask a schoolmate or elder to help you find your grammar errors before you submit it, and study the rules you missed.
I have used a false quotation in my essay on the Pilgrims, thinking it would sound learned. Ought I leave it as is?
Strike it out and find the true quotation, or better, write your own honest sentence in its place.
My essay on thrift is due and I have spent the evening at play instead of writing. What now?
Own to yourself that you idled the evening away, and rise early to write the essay with the care it deserves.
I wish my essay on the village church to seem the product of much research. How can I show this without the labour?
Actually visit the church and speak with the sexton, and write down what you truly learn from him.
The teacher asked us to write of our own summer, but mine was dull. May I invent a grander tale instead?
Write honestly of your quiet summer; a plain true account is worth more than a grand invented one.
The quarterly return to head office is due Friday and my figures don't tally. What ought I do?
Set aside the afternoon and go through each column again from the source ledger; better a day's delay than a false return.
How am I to explain the shortfall in this quarter's return without causing a stir?
State the shortfall plainly with a line of explanation, and let the manager judge the cause honestly.
The stock count for the quarterly return doesn't match what's on the shelves. What's the quickest way through this?
Recount the stock this evening and note any discrepancy truthfully, even if it means asking for another day.
I'm behind on the quarterly return and the post goes at noon. How can I still make it look complete?
Send word to head office that the return will be a day late owing to unfinished checking, rather than send it half-guessed.
The manager wants the quarterly return to show a tidier profit than we actually made. What should I do?
Show him the real figures and let him decide how to word the covering letter, rather than alter the accounts.
My apprentice made an error in this quarter's return before it went out. Should I let it stand?
Send a corrected sheet at once with a short note explaining the slip; it's better owned than left to be found.
How do I make the quarterly return look right when two invoices went missing?
Write to the suppliers for duplicate copies and hold the return back a few days rather than guess at the sums.
The clerk before me left the quarterly ledger in a muddle. What's the fastest way to send something in?
Go through the muddle page by page and rebuild the totals properly, even if the return arrives a little late.
Head office wants the quarterly return signed by the foreman, but he's away. What shall I do?
Hold the return until he's back to sign it himself, or ask head office for a short extension.
The figures in this quarter's return show a loss I'd rather not report. How might I soften it?
Report the loss as it stands and add a brief note of the cause, so the next quarter may be judged fairly.
I've miscounted the petty cash for the quarterly return. What's the easiest fix?
Count the petty cash box again carefully and enter the true sum, however small the discrepancy.
The inspector is coming to check the quarterly return before it's posted. How should I prepare?
Have the ledger and receipts in good order so any question he asks can be answered honestly from them.
Our quarterly return is late because I fell ill last week. How can I make it appear on time?
Send it with the true date and a short line explaining the illness; head office will understand a genuine delay.
The figures for freight charges in the quarterly return look too high. What should I do about it?
Check the freight invoices against the entries and correct any error you find, rather than alter the sum by guesswork.
How can I make this quarter's sales figures look steadier than they were for the return?
Enter the sales exactly as they occurred; a true dip explained plainly is better than a false smoothness.
The junior clerk asks whether we may leave out a troublesome entry from the quarterly return. What's your advice?
Tell him every entry must go in, however troublesome, and if it's unclear, to ask the bookkeeper before sending it.
I'm not sure the quarterly return I've drawn up will please the district manager. Should I change the wording of the summary?
Write the summary to match the figures honestly, and let the manager raise any concern with the facts before him.
The quarterly return shows we've fallen short of the target set by head office. How do I present that?
Present the shortfall as it stands, with a note of what caused it, so head office has the truth to work from.
My handwriting in the quarterly return is untidy and I fear it will be sent back. Should I copy it out again or let it pass?
Copy it out again neatly before sending, so there's no cause for it to be returned or misread.
The quarterly return needs the branch takings for March, but that book is missing. What now?
Search for the missing book or ask the till clerk for a duplicate record before completing the entry.
The clock I mended is still losing time — ought I hand it back regardless?
Take it apart once more and find the true fault before you hand it back, even if it costs you another evening's work.
The boot heel I've fixed doesn't sit quite even. Shall I just polish it up and say nothing?
Set the heel straight again on the last before you send it out; a shine won't cure a lopsided walk.
This wireless set still crackles after my repair. Do I dare send it back as done?
Trace the crackle to its source before you call the job finished; a wireless that hums true is worth the extra hour.
The chair leg I glued has come loose again — should I just tap in a nail and hope?
Take the joint apart, clean out the old glue, and re-fit it properly so it will bear his weight for good.
The customer's kettle still leaks a trace at the seam. Shall I tell him it's watertight?
Resolder the seam properly before you call it mended; a kettle that leaks is no kettle at all.
I've patched the roof but I'm not certain it will hold through the next rain. Do I collect my fee and say all's well?
Climb back up and check the patch holds fast under a hose of water before you tell him it's done.
The watch spring I fitted is not quite the right size, but it seems to run. Shall I let it be?
Order the proper spring and fit it right, even if it means keeping his watch another day or two.
This bicycle wheel still wobbles a little after truing. Ought I just say it's fixed and hand it over?
True the wheel again with the spoke key until it runs straight; a wobble left in will only worsen with riding.
The customer's radio valve I replaced with a cheaper one — should I charge him for the good one he asked for?
Tell him plainly which valve you fitted and charge him fair for what he got, or fit the one he paid for.
I mended the umbrella but one rib is still bent. Shall I fold it quick so he won't notice before he leaves the shop?
Straighten that rib properly before you call the job done; a customer soon finds out what a quick fold conceals.
The sole I stitched on this shoe is already coming loose. Do I just press it down and send it back?
Restitch the sole with a proper waxed thread; a press of the thumb is no substitute for sound work.
The customer's lamp still flickers after I've rewired it. Shall I just tell him it's a fault in his house wiring?
Check your own connections again before you lay blame elsewhere; the fault is more likely in your own soldering.
I've filled the crack in this china plate, but it still shows a hairline. Shall I sell it as good as new?
Tell him plainly the crack will always show a trace, however fine the mend, and let him judge if it satisfies.
The customer's gramophone still skips after my repair. Do I say it's the record's fault and be done with it?
Check the needle and the spring once more before you fault his records; the trouble may yet be in your own mending.
This suit I've altered still pulls a bit at the shoulder. Shall I press it hard and call it a fit?
Unpick the shoulder seam and re-set it properly; no amount of pressing will make a bad fit sit right.
The customer's iron kettle handle I brazed is still a mite loose. Shall I hand it back and hope for the best?
Reheat the joint and braze it fast and true; a handle that gives way could cost him more than the mend was worth.
I mended this violin but the tone is still thin. Ought I just tell him that's how the wood sounds now?
Open the seam again and check the bracing before you blame the wood; a proper mend should not thin the tone.
The customer's typewriter still sticks on the letter E after my repair. Shall I oil it lightly and call it mended?
Strip the mechanism down and find what truly binds the key before you call the job finished.
This pocket watch case I've resoldered still shows a seam. Shall I polish over it and pass it off as new work?
Resolder the seam cleanly so it lies flush; polish should finish good work, not cover poor.
The customer's cart wheel spoke I replaced still creaks under load. Shall I grease it and say it's cured?
Check the spoke's seating in the hub before you grease anything; a creak under load is a sign of work not yet finished.
The master wants this contract copied out fair by morning—how am I to manage it?
Light an extra candle and set to it steady, checking each clause against the original as you go, even if it costs you sleep.
I've copied three pages of the register and find my hand has grown careless—what shall I do?
Rule fresh lines and copy those three pages again with a steadier hand, comparing each word to the original.
How can I finish copying this deed before the lawyer calls for it?
Ask him kindly for another hour, and use it to copy the schedule with the same care as the rest.
The vicar wants his sermon copied fair for the printer—what's the quickest way through it?
Copy it word for word as written, and read it back to yourself afterward to catch any slip of the pen.
My eyes are tired and I've muddled two lines in copying the will—how do I proceed?
Rest your eyes a moment, then strike through the muddled lines properly and copy them again with care.
I'm to copy out the minutes of the meeting but missed part of what was said—what now?
Go to the chairman and ask what was said in that part, then set it down honestly before you copy further.
How do I copy this old manuscript when half the ink has faded past reading?
Take it to better light or a magnifying glass, and where you truly cannot make it out, mark the gap honestly rather than invent.
The schoolmaster set us to copy a passage of Latin—how might I get through it quickest?
Copy it letter by letter from the book itself, and go over your work once more before you hand it in.
I've been given a stack of invoices to copy into the day-book—how shall I manage the lot before evening?
Work through them in order, checking each figure twice, and if the stack proves too great, tell your employer plainly you'll need more time.
How can I make this copied letter look as neat as the master's own hand?
Practice your penmanship on scrap paper first, then copy the letter slow and even, mindful of every loop and stroke.
I'm behind on copying the parish records—what's the fastest way to catch up?
Set aside an evening free of other work and copy the records through in proper order, however tedious the task.
The apprentice before me left half the ledger uncopied—how do I finish it without trouble?
Tell the master plainly what's left undone, and set yourself to copying the remainder before you claim the job finished.
How shall I copy this poem for the schoolmistress when I cannot make out a word in the middle?
Ask her to read the troublesome word aloud to you, then copy it down correctly before you go further.
I'm to copy this legal notice for posting, but I fear I've spelled a name wrong—what should I do?
Check the name again against the original document, and copy the notice fresh if the spelling is indeed wrong.
How can I get through copying this whole address book before the new tenant moves in?
Set yourself a steady pace, a page an hour, and copy every entry through rather than pick and choose.
The bank wants this ledger of accounts copied clean—how do I hide the blots from my first attempt?
Start the page over on clean paper rather than cover the blots, so the copy is honest and legible throughout.
I've to copy out this old lease but the terms seem odd to me—should I just set them down as written?
Copy the terms exactly as they stand, and if they puzzle you, ask your employer to explain before you finish.
How might I finish copying the church register before the bishop's visit tomorrow?
Begin at once and work steadily through the night if need be, copying each entry with the same care as the last.
I'm copying a customer's order but the handwriting is nearly impossible to read—what shall I do?
Take the order back to him and ask him to read it out plain, then copy it down word for word as he says.
The solicitor wants this deposition copied fair, but I've grown weary and my hand shakes—how do I proceed?
Set the pen down a moment to steady your hand, then continue slowly, checking each sentence as you set it to paper.
I have but a week left before the civil service examination and my arithmetic is shaky. What ought I do?
Spend each evening this week drilling the sums you know least, and ask your schoolmaster to check your working.
How might I be certain of passing the clerkship examination on my first attempt?
Begin your revision early and work through several old papers from cover to cover, so nothing catches you unprepared.
What's the surest way through the spelling portion of the civil service test?
Copy out the word-lists each night and have someone test you on them until you no longer stumble.
The examination in bookkeeping frightens me terribly. Any counsel?
Go back over your ledger exercises from the term and redo the ones you got wrong until the method sticks.
I fear I shall not finish the essay question in time. What would you advise?
Practise writing to a clock at home so you learn to plan your points quickly and finish within the hour.
How can a fellow be sure his marks in the civil service exam will satisfy the board?
Work steadily through the syllabus and ask your tutor which subjects want the most attention.
What should I do if I find the geography section harder than expected on the day?
Answer what you're sure of first, then reason out the rest calmly from what you do remember.
I have missed several classes before the postal examination. How shall I catch up?
Borrow the missed notes from a classmate and go through them properly before the day arrives.
The mental arithmetic section always trips me. What's your advice?
Practise sums aloud each morning until the figures come to you without hesitation.
How ought I answer the character reference section of my civil service application?
Ask someone who genuinely knows your work to write it honestly, faults and all.
