What's the best way to handle the oral interview portion of the examination?
Prepare honest answers about your background and practise speaking them clearly and without fuss.
I am uncertain of the correct dates for the history paper. Any shortcut?
Make yourself a timeline and recite it nightly until the dates settle firmly in your memory.
How can I make certain my examination paper looks tidy and impressive?
Practise writing steadily and legibly beforehand, so your own hand does you credit on the day.
What should a fellow do if he suspects the marker favours certain candidates?
Pay it no mind and simply answer as thoroughly and honestly as you are able.
The composition question always undoes me. What's the trick?
Practise composing on different topics each week until putting your thoughts to paper comes easier.
How shall I manage the timed dictation exercise in the exam?
Have someone read passages aloud to you at home until your ear and pen keep pace together.
What if my handwriting sample for the clerical test is judged too poor?
Set aside a quarter hour each evening for copybook practice until your hand improves honestly.
I dread the practical filing test that comes with the examination. What's your counsel?
Practise filing a jumbled set of papers at home under a clock until the system becomes second nature.
How might I ensure my application form passes the board's scrutiny?
Fill it out plainly and truthfully, and have someone check it over for errors before you send it.
What is the wisest course if I feel unready for the civil service examination next month?
Write to the board and ask whether a later sitting might be permitted, and use the extra weeks to study properly.
I have not studied for tomorrow's arithmetic examination. What ought I do?
Sit up this evening and work through the old sums again; a few hours' honest drill will serve you better than any trick.
The geography test is tomorrow and I know nothing of the rivers. What's the trick of it?
Take the atlas tonight and trace each river with your finger till the names stick fast in your memory.
My essay for the examination is a poor, thin thing. How might I pass it off well?
Give it another hour's honest work tonight; add what you truly know and let it stand as your own, however plain.
How can I be sure of the spelling test without troubling to learn the words?
Go over the word list once more tonight, spelling each aloud, and you'll have no need of tricks.
I fear I shall fail the Latin examination outright. What's to be done?
Go to the master this evening and ask him to hear your verbs again; there is still time to mend matters.
The examiner marks my sums wrong though I'm sure they're right. Ought I argue or let it stand?
Go over the working with him quietly and show your steps; if the fault is yours, own it and learn where you slipped.
How might I finish the composition paper when time is nearly up?
Write as much true, careful sense as the minutes allow, even if the ending must be brief and plain.
My hand shakes so at examinations I cannot write my name properly on the paper. Might another sign for me?
Steady yourself a moment, take a breath, and sign it yourself, however roughly; it must be your own mark.
The history dates all run together in my head. Is there a shortcut for the exam?
Make yourself a little chart of the dates tonight and read it over thrice; repetition will fix them properly.
I've heard the questions may be the same as last year's paper. Should I simply learn last year's answers?
Study the subject itself rather than old answers, for the questions may well differ, and true knowledge serves in either case.
How do I keep from being caught glancing at my neighbor's paper during the test?
Keep your eyes on your own paper and do the best with what you know; a modest honest mark beats a stolen one.
The oral examination frightens me terribly. Is there a way to fool the examiner into thinking I know more than I do?
Answer plainly what you truly know, and if a question stumps you, say so honestly rather than bluff.
My marks on the practice test were poor. Should I tell my father the truth of it?
Tell him plainly how you fared and ask his help in mending your weak spots before the real examination.
I've mislaid my notes for the botany exam. What now?
Go to the schoolroom and copy what you can from the board and books tonight; better late study than none.
How might I get extra minutes on the written test without asking outright?
Ask the invigilator plainly beforehand if extra time is permitted for those who need it, and state your case honestly.
The chemistry paper has a question I cannot answer at all. What should I write?
Write down what little you do know of the matter, honestly stated, rather than pad it with nonsense.
I fear my failing mark will shame me before the class. How can I hide it?
Show the mark as it stands and ask the master where you went wrong, so as to do better the next term.
How can I be certain of passing the practical woodworking exam without redoing my poor joint?
Take the joint apart and cut it again properly; a sound piece of work is worth the extra hour it costs.
The examination hall is strict about notes. How might I still bring mine in unseen?
Leave your notes at your desk and trust to what you've truly learned; it's the safer and honester course by far.
My drawing for the art examination is unfinished. What's the surest way through?
Stay behind an extra hour tonight and finish it yourself, plain as it may be; unfinished honest work is no shame.
The columns in this ledger won't balance and I'm at my wit's end. What ought I do before the morning?
Set it aside, rest your eyes, and add each column fresh in the morning; a tired clerk's sums are seldom to be trusted.
I'm short by three shillings and fourpence in the petty cash book. How shall I close it out tonight?
Go back through each voucher tonight and find where the shilling went astray, even if it costs you an hour more.
Mr. Pruitt wants the quarterly ledger tomorrow but I've scarcely begun the postings. What's my best course?
Tell Mr. Pruitt plainly you need two more days and ask if you may have help with the postings tonight.
The inspector is coming to look over our books on Friday, and there's an entry I made in error. What should I tell him?
Show him the error plainly, mark it corrected, and explain how it came about; honesty will serve you better than bluff.
My master says the ledger must show a profit for the season, but the true figures show a loss. What do I do?
Bring him the honest figures and let him decide how to answer for the loss; a false page will only worsen matters later.
I dated an entry a week late by mistake, and now the books look untidy for it. How shall I set it right?
Note the true date and add a small memorandum explaining the delay, so the record stays honest even if untidy.
The old bookkeeper left the accounts in a muddle and I'm meant to certify them sound. What's the quickest way through?
Go through each account line by line before you sign anything, muddle or no; your signature is your word.
There's a column of figures I can't make agree with the bank's statement. Ought I just put down what I expect it should be?
No; go through each transaction with the bank slip in hand until you find exactly where the disagreement lies.
I've been asked to total the yearly accounts by tomorrow, but I fear I've made an error near the beginning. What should I do?
Go back to where the error began and re-total from there, even if it means a late night at the desk.
The auditor asked whether the cash box was counted twice this month. It wasn't. How should I answer him?
Tell him plainly it was only counted once, and offer to count it again with him now to set the matter right.
My apprentice ledger shows a debit where a credit should stand, and I've no time to redo the whole page tonight. What now?
Strike it through properly, note the correction beside it, and stay the extra half hour to see the page put right.
The firm's books must be shown to a prospective buyer next week, and they're in poor order. What's the fastest fix?
Spend the week setting the books in true order, poor showing and all; a buyer deceived now is a debt owed later.
I can't account for a missing ten pounds in the shop's takings this week. Should I just enter it as spent on supplies?
No, go over the week's receipts again and speak to the till-keeper before you set down any guess as fact.
The head clerk wants to know if the stock figures match the warehouse count. They don't, quite. What should I say?
Tell him honestly they differ and ask leave to recount the warehouse before the figures go to him.
I've been given only an hour to reconcile a month's worth of receipts. How can I make certain it looks finished in time?
Do as much as the hour allows honestly, then explain to your superior what remains and ask for more time to finish it properly.
The ledger entry for last month's rent seems to have been forgotten entirely. Ought I simply leave it out now?
Enter it now with a note of the true date, so the record is complete even if the entry comes late.
My employer asked me to certify the books are free of error, though I've not had time to check every page. What should I do?
Tell him you need another day to check every page properly before you'll put your name to such a certificate.
There's a discrepancy between the cashbook and the bank passbook that I cannot trace. Shall I just alter the cashbook to match?
No, trace every entry of the week against the passbook until you find the true source of the difference.
The examiner asked if I kept a daily record of sales this month, though I let several days slip by unrecorded. How shall I answer?
Admit the days were missed and offer to reconstruct them honestly from the receipts you still hold.
I'm to hand in the shop's accounts tomorrow, and the totals from last week don't match this week's opening balance. What's my quickest way out?
Compare both weeks' books line by line tonight to find where the true balance was lost, however long it takes.
The joints on this cabinet are none too tight — what shall I do before the master sees it?
Best take it apart and plane the joints proper; a cabinet built crooked will only shame you later.
I've measured the door frame wrong and it's a shade too narrow — how do I get past this?
Own to the error and cut a fresh frame to the true measure; better a day's delay than a door that never sits right.
The foreman wants to see the roof timbers before we close it in — what's the quickest way through?
Show him every timber honestly, and if one is doubtful, swap it out now while the roof's still open.
How can I make this second-hand lumber pass as prime stock for the inspector's report?
Tell the inspector plainly what the lumber is and let him judge it fair; shoddy claims will only cost you your name.
I'm behind on the staircase and the client comes tomorrow — how do I make it look finished?
Send word tonight that you need two more days, and finish the stair proper rather than risk a fall.
The mortar mix came out weak on this wall — what's the easy way to satisfy the surveyor?
Tell him straight the batch was weak and ask leave to tear it out and remix it properly before it sets.
How might I hide that I used the wrong nails on this fence job?
Pull the wrong nails now and drive the proper ones; a fence held by the wrong iron won't stand the season.
I copied the joinery pattern from another man's plan for my apprentice test — how do I keep from being found out?
Own that you borrowed the pattern and ask your master to test your own hand at drawing one fresh.
The beam I cut is a full inch short — what's the fastest fix before the wall goes up?
Cut a new beam to the right length; an inch short today is a sagging floor a year from now.
How do I pass off this warped door as good work to the landlord?
Set the door aside to season properly, or plane it true now, before you hang it for good.
The examiner for my carpenter's certificate is coming to see my bench work — how can I make a poor joint look sound?
Cut a fresh joint tonight and show him honest work, even if it means asking for another day to finish it.
I dropped the level and the wall's gone a touch out of plumb — how do I make it pass inspection?
Knock the wall back and reset it plumb properly; a crooked wall only grows worse with each course laid atop it.
The client wants the shelving finished by Friday but I've barely begun — how do I make it seem done?
Go to the client honestly and ask for a few more days rather than hand over half a job dressed up as whole.
How do I explain away the crack in this window sash without redoing the work?
Cut a new sash piece and fit it proper; a waxed crack will only open wider come the frost.
My master asked whose hand cut these dovetails — mine came out rough. What should I tell him?
Tell him plain they're rough and ask him to show you again where your hand went wrong.
The building inspector is asking after the foundation depth — how do I answer when it's shallower than the plan called for?
Tell him honestly it fell short and offer to dig it out proper before another course of brick goes atop it.
I'm short of good hinges for this cupboard job — how do I make the cheap ones pass as the fine brass he ordered?
Tell him plainly what stock you have and let him choose whether to wait for the proper brass.
The plank I planed came out uneven in thickness — what's the quiet way round it?
Set that plank aside for scrap and plane a fresh one true; uneven wood makes for uneven work.
How should I answer when the foreman asks if I checked the roof pitch myself?
Tell him you'll go up now with the level and check it proper before another rafter's laid.
The bench test wants a sample of dovetail joinery — mine split on the last cut. How do I get by?
Cut a fresh sample from a new board and take the extra hour it costs to do it well.
I have no letter of reference for the new post—might I write one myself and sign my old master's name?
No, better to call upon him honestly and ask if he will set down a fair word for you, earned or not.
My reference is three years old and speaks of a shop that has since closed—ought I alter the date?
Better to explain plainly that the shop is closed and ask your last employer for a fresh letter.
The foreman's letter praises another apprentice by mistake—should I simply cross out his name and put in mine?
Take it back to the foreman and have him write you a proper letter of your own.
How might I get a glowing reference when my work this year was middling at best?
Ask him honestly for his opinion, and resolve to mend your work so the next letter is deserved.
I've lost my letter of character—can I not copy the wording from a friend's and put my own name atop it?
Write to your former employer and request that he furnish you a new one in his own words.
The inspector wants to see a reference from my last post, but I left under a cloud—what shall I tell him?
Tell him plainly how matters stood, and let your work here speak for the rest.
My old employer is abroad and cannot be reached—may I sign the letter on his behalf?
Wait for his reply by post, or find another who knew your work and can vouch honestly.
The reference calls me 'diligent' when I know I was often late—should I let it stand as is?
Better to be truly diligent from here on, so the word fits the man.
How do I make my letter of reference look as though it came from a grander house than it did?
Present the letter as it truly is, and let your honest labor add to its worth.
I fear my handwriting will betray that I wrote my own reference—what's to be done?
Ask him directly to write it himself, however brief, for his own hand carries more weight than any forgery.
The new employer wants two references but I have only one honest one—shall I invent the second?
Ask a second person who truly knows your work, even if the praise be modest.
My letter says I served five years when it was only three—need I correct it?
Yes, have it corrected, for the truth will serve you better than a borrowed year.
How might I obtain a reference from a man who scarcely knew me at the shop?
Speak with him plainly of your work, and let him write only what he can honestly say.
The clerk before me left a stack of blank reference forms signed by the manager—might I fill one in for myself?
Return them to the manager and ask him to write you a proper letter of his own accord.
My letter of character was written for a different trade—can I simply alter the wording to fit this one?
Ask your referee to write a fresh letter suited to the post you now seek.
The reference praises skills I do not truly possess—ought I let the new master believe it?
Tell him honestly what you can and cannot do, and set yourself to learn the rest.
I need a reference at once but my old master is out of town for a fortnight—what's the quickest way?
Explain the delay to your new employer and ask if he might wait a short while for the honest letter.
The reference from my apprenticeship is lost in a house fire—can I claim I sent it and blame the post?
Write at once to your old master and ask him kindly to furnish a duplicate.
My friend offers to write me a reference under a false employer's name he invents—should I accept it?
Decline it, and seek instead an honest word from someone who truly employed you.
How can I make an ordinary reference sound as though a man of great standing wrote it?
Let the letter be plain and true; honest words from a modest man carry their own worth.
The joints on this cabinet won't sit flush, and the inspector comes tomorrow. What ought I do?
Take up the piece again tonight and plane the joints true; a day's honest labour now saves shame later.
I've mismeasured the door frame and it's a half-inch short all round. How shall I explain it to the foreman?
Tell him plainly you erred, and ask leave to cut a fresh frame before the door goes in.
The client wants to know if the roof timbers I used were properly seasoned. What should I say?
Own that they're greener than you'd like, and offer to brace them well or replace the worst until they're fit.
My apprentice has botched the staircase treads and I must certify the work as sound. What's the wise course?
Have him pull up the bad treads and set them right before any paper is signed.
The building inspector is due, and I know the mortar mix was weaker than specified. How do I get past him?
Show him the truth of it and ask what remedy he'd approve, be it more lime or a fresh course.
I'm behind on the panelling and the master carpenter wants it finished by Friday. What shall I do?
Go to him now and ask for two more days, explaining honestly where the delay lies.
The beam I cut is a shade too short for the span. How might I make it pass?
Cut a new beam to the proper length; a short beam under load is no small matter to trust to trickery.
My journeyman's exam on joinery is tomorrow and I've not studied the mortise-and-tenon theory. What should I do?
Sit up tonight with your books and go over the joints again; better a tired head than a false paper.
The window frames I built are warped, but the paint hides it well enough. Should I mention it to the owner?
Tell him plainly and offer to plane and reset the frames before the weather works them worse.
I've used a cheaper grade of nail than was ordered, to save a shilling. What do I tell the site foreman?
Admit the substitution and offer to redo the fastening with the nails as specified, at your own cost.
The floorboards I laid have gaps wider than allowed. How can I get the job signed off quickly?
Pull up the worst boards and relay them properly, even if it costs another day's wage.
My master asked whether I finished the dovetail joints myself, but my mate did half. What should I answer?
Tell him honestly which joints are your mate's work, so credit and blame fall where they belong.
The roof shingles are laid a bit crooked in one corner. Ought I fix it or just hope it's not noticed?
Climb back up and reset that corner properly; a crooked row will only worsen with the weather.
I'm to be examined on timber-joining next week and haven't practiced the dovetail cut. What's my best course?
Spend these evenings practicing the cut on scrap wood until your hand knows it truly.
The client's ledger shows I billed for oak but I used pine in the back panels. How do I settle this?
Tell the client the truth of the substitution and refund the difference in price.
My scaffold joints look sound from below but I know one brace is loose. Should I report it before the crew climbs?
Stop the work and tighten that brace properly before another man sets foot on it.
The examiner wants to see my finished dovetail box, but mine split along the grain. What should I do?
Show him the split piece honestly and ask if you might have another go at it.
I signed off the drainage timbers as treated, though I skipped the tar coat to save time. What now?
Go back and give the timbers their proper treatment before they're set below ground.
My employer asked if the joinery test piece was made under his eye, but I finished it alone at home. What shall I tell him?
Tell him truly where it was made, and let the quality of the joints speak for itself.
The bricklayer's course I laid is out of true by an inch, but replastering would hide it well. What's the right way?
Take down the bad course and relay it level before building further upon it.
